description: One note a worker wrote from inside the handset app: what they were looking at, what they said, who they were, and when they pressed Send. The bubble is on every screen and the form auto-captures the rest, so what a reader gets is a complaint with its context already attached rather than 'the app is broken'. entry_uuid is the dedup key and is unique: the phone queues every note locally and drains the backlog in one pass the first time the route answers, so a worker's considered complaint must not be able to arrive three times. timestamp is when Send was pressed and received_at is when it landed, which on a farm with no signal in the blocks may be weeks apart — the feed is sorted on the first, because that is the recency a reader means.
name: App Feedback

fields.description: The series a note is named from, EXPANDED BY THE CONTROLLER rather than by Frappe's naming_series hook — the same split Bucket Log Entry and Farm Shift keep, and here the reason is sharper than on either. Frappe expands `.YYYY.` from the date of the INSERT, and this is the one register where the insert and the event routinely differ by weeks: a phone with no signal in the blocks holds a note until it finds the yard's wifi. The year is the SUBMISSION's, so a note written on 31 December and drained on 2 January is filed under the season it was written in. The field is here so the Desk shows what the shape is meant to be.
fields.label: Series

fields.description: The handset's own UUID for this note. THE DEDUP KEY, and unique for that reason rather than as tidiness. Nothing could drain until this route existed, so the first successful drain replays a backlog that may be weeks deep in one pass — and twice if it is interrupted. submit_app_feedback answers with the record it already holds instead of writing a second one; the unique index is what makes that safe when two drains race each other.
fields.label: Entry UUID

fields.description: Which screen the bubble was tapped on, as a stable ASCII key — my_tasks, harvest_day, bucket_capture. NEVER TRANSLATED, which is what makes it a filter: a feed grouped by what the app calls the screen answers 'which part of this is people struggling with', and a feed grouped by a Spanish label and an English label for one screen answers nothing.
fields.label: Screen

fields.description: The English name of that screen, for a reader. Display only — nothing filters or groups on it, because it is the half that moves when somebody retitles a tab.
fields.label: Screen Label

fields.description: The kind of record the worker was looking at when they wrote this, as the app names it (Item, Spray REI, MRL Record ...). Optional, and stored as sent rather than checked: a note about a record somebody has since renamed or deleted is still worth reading, and a refused note is re-sent by the phone forever.
fields.label: Reference DocType

fields.description: Which one: the docname of the product, block or record on the screen. With Reference DocType it answers 'which product is this note about' without anyone reading the screenshot.
fields.label: Reference Name

fields.description: The note. THE ONLY THING THE WORKER TYPED — everything else on this record was captured for them, which is the whole design of the bubble: somebody in gloves standing in a row should be able to say the thing and put the phone away.
fields.label: Feedback

fields.description: What the person was reading when they wrote it. Not a guess from the text: the app knows which language it was rendering, and a note in English written on a Spanish interface is a different fact from one written on an English one.
fields.label: Language

fields.description: Whether the microphone produced any of it. THE MEASUREMENT THAT SAYS WHETHER THE GLOVES-ON PATH IS USED — dictation was built for a crew that cannot type in the field, and this column is the only way to find out whether that was right.
fields.label: Dictated

fields.description: Who wrote it, RESOLVED FROM THE AUTHENTICATED CALLER and never from the request body. A shared handset is normal here, so the app sends its own idea of who is holding the phone; that idea is a claim and it is kept in claimed_employee, while this column is the one a join, a filter or a follow-up conversation can rely on. Empty where the caller has no Employee record yet — the note is still filed, because a login without an Employee row is exactly the kind of person whose feedback is worth reading.
fields.label: Employee

fields.description: Denormalised from employee so the feed reads as names rather than HR-EMP-00007.
fields.label: Employee Name

fields.description: The role the person was acting as in the app when they wrote it. THE APP'S CLAIM, KEPT AS ONE, and it is stored anyway because it is half of what the owner filters by: 'every complaint a foreman filed about dispatch' is a question the server cannot reconstruct after the fact, since one login can hold several roles and the app knows which hat was on. It authorises nothing — no gate on this site reads this column.
fields.label: Role

fields.description: The job title the handset reported, if it sent one. A claim, like role, and kept for the same reason: it is what somebody reading the feed needs to know whether a complaint about the crew board came from the person who runs it.
fields.label: Designation

fields.description: The login this note actually arrived under, written from the authenticated session. The one identity on this record that was proved rather than reported.
fields.label: User

fields.description: The Employee docname the handset named, stored ONLY when it disagrees with the resolved employee — which is what a shared handset looks like from here. Data rather than a Link on purpose: a claim that a link validated would refuse the note over somebody else's typo, and the point of keeping it is to be able to see that the two differed.
fields.label: Claimed Employee

fields.description: The name that went with claimed_employee, on the same terms.
fields.label: Claimed Employee Name

fields.description: Which operation the note belongs to, resolved against the caller's own entities. Optional: a note is never refused for failing to name a company, because a complaint that cannot be filed is the one outcome this whole route exists to end.
fields.label: Company

fields.description: When the person pressed Send. NOT WHEN THE NOTE ARRIVED, which may be weeks later on a farm whose blocks have no signal. The list sorts on this because it is the recency a reader means: the newest complaint is the one most recently made, not the one most recently synced.
fields.label: Submitted At

fields.description: When this site received it. The distance between this and timestamp is how long the note sat in a pocket, which is worth being able to see when somebody asks why nobody acted on it.
fields.label: Received At

fields.description: The app build the note was written on. A filter column, because the commonest useful question about a pile of feedback is whether the complaints stop at a version.
fields.label: App Version

fields.description: The utsname machine identifier — iPhone17,2 — and not UIDevice.model's bare 'iPhone'. The distinction is the whole value of the column: 'only on the old handsets' is an answer, 'only on iPhones' is not.
fields.label: Device Model

fields.description: The handset's own stable identifier, the same one the push register keys on. It is what makes 'this one phone produces every complaint about the scanner' a question somebody can ask.
fields.label: Device ID

fields.description: Whether a screenshot came with the note. Kept in step with the screenshot field by the controller and never set by a caller, so it is a filter a reader can trust — 'show me the ones with a picture' should not depend on a client having remembered to tick a box.
fields.label: Has Screenshot

fields.description: Why there is no picture on a note that was written with one. The handset drops a capture that came out over its own inline ceiling and sends the reason instead of the bytes, because the note matters more than the screenshot and refusing the whole submission over an oversized JPEG would park the complaint forever. Empty on a note that never had one — 'the worker did not take a screenshot' and 'the screenshot did not fit' are different facts, and only the second one is somebody's bug.
fields.label: Screenshot Omitted

fields.description: The optional capture, stored as a PRIVATE File. Private is not a choice a caller gets to make: a screenshot of the app is a screenshot of whatever roster, wage or task list was on the screen at the time, and a public File is readable by anybody who can guess the URL.
fields.label: Screenshot

fields.description: Whether anybody has answered this note. DEFAULTS TO OPEN AND IS NEVER SET BY THE HANDSET — a worker files a complaint, and whether it was acted on is a statement the farm makes about itself. "Won't Fix" is a real answer and is deliberately not spelled "Closed": the difference between "we did this" and "we are not going to" is the whole of what somebody reading the feed a season later needs to know.
fields.label: Status

fields.description: What was done, or why it will not be. Required by `resolve_app_feedback` for "Won't Fix" and optional for "Resolved", because a note refused with no reason is the thing that stops people filing the next one.
fields.label: Resolution Note

fields.description: The account that answered it, written from the session rather than from the body — an answer filed in somebody else's name is worse than an unanswered note.
fields.label: Resolved By
